papers.version_note: Web page text from the Quantum Computing Inc resource library, dated May 15, 2024, labeled Policy Paper. The text carries site navigation before and after the article body. The page cites no sources.
papers.what_it_is: A one-page vendor policy paper in which Quantum Computing Inc promotes thin film lithium niobate as a platform for telecom and photonic computing and describes its planned Tempe, Arizona fabrication facility.

assertions.value: The page is dated May 15, 2024 and labeled Policy Paper by Quantum Computing Inc.
quotes: Thin Film Lithium Niobate (TFLN) May 15, 2024 Policy Paper
assertions.certainty_reason: The page states its own date and document type.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no citations, data tables or methods, so every figure in it is an unsourced vendor statement.

assertions.value: The authors state that modulators built using TFLN consume very little power and can operate at approximately 250 Gbaud with lower insertion losses than most other contenders. No measurement or source is given.
quotes: Modulators built using TFLN are not only highly efficient since they consume very little power
capable of operating with an extremely high bandwidth (approximately 250 Gbaud) and with lower insertion losses compared to most other contenders
assertions.certainty_reason: A general performance claim from a vendor with no data or citation in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that there is growing consensus in the telecommunications and hyperscale industries that TFLN will become a key enabler of 1.6 and 3.2 terabit optical switches and interconnects. No survey or source is cited.
quotes: there is growing consensus in the telecommunications and hyperscale industries that TFLN will become a key enabler of the 1.6 and 3.2 terabit optical switches and interconnects
assertions.certainty_reason: An unsourced claim of industry consensus.

assertions.value: The authors state that TFLN devices hold the promise of significantly reducing overall device size, which would help heterogeneous integration and optical packaging.
quotes: TFLN devices hold the promise of significantly reducing the overall device size, thereby further aiding the long-heralded heterogeneous integration and optical packaging
assertions.certainty_reason: A forward-looking promise with no data in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that TFLN is highly nonlinear and efficient, is useful for switching and modulation, creates minimal amounts of noise, and has wide and efficient optical bandwidth.
quotes: TFLN is special because it is highly nonlinear and efficient, useful for switching and modulation, creates minimal amounts of noise, and has wide and efficient optical bandwidth.
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement of material properties with no measurement or source in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that the current market for TFLN is $190 million and is projected to grow at a CAGR of 39.2% to $1.93 billion by 2029, driven by demand in telecom, hyper-scaling and artificial intelligence, and RF communications. No source for the projection is given.
quotes: The current market for TFLN is $190 million and is projected to grow at a CAGR of 39.2% to $1.93 billion by 2029.
This growth is driven by the demand in the telecom, hyper-scaling and artificial intelligence, and RF communications industries.
assertions.certainty_reason: A market forecast with no cited source or method.
assertions.reader_inference: The stated figures are internally consistent as a growth path, but the page does not name who made the projection.

assertions.value: The authors state that a six-inch TFLN chip can yield over $3 million in revenue. No basis for the figure is given.
quotes: TFLN is already highly valuable, and a six-inch chip can yield over $3 million in revenue.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unsourced revenue figure with no stated assumptions.

assertions.value: The authors state that TFLN is available only in limited supply, coming directly from China, and that few large-scale semiconductor companies have deployed TFLN lines because the supply chain is limited.
quotes: Currently, TFLN is only available in limited supply, coming directly from China, because it is extremely difficult to create or
Because the supply chain is so limited, large-scale semiconductor companies have not yet deployed TFLN lines.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unsourced statement about the supply chain. The text states that no large-scale semiconductor company has yet deployed TFLN lines.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Computing Inc is the only company in the United States capable of processing 150mm wafers, and that its TFLN fab is equipped with both front and backend optical packaging capabilities.
quotes: is the only company in the United States capable of processing 150mm wafers
The QCi TFLN fab is equipped with both front and as well as backend optical packaging capabilities
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own capability with no independent source in the page.

assertions.value: The authors state that Quantum Computing Inc will open a fully commissioned TFLN fabrication facility by Q1 2025 in Tempe, Arizona, and that in the first full year of production it will be capable of producing over $180M in sellable product.
quotes: QCi will open a fully commissioned TFLN fabrication facility by Q1 2025 in Tempe, Arizona.
In the first full year of production, the company will be capable of producing over $180M in sellable product.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's forward-looking plan for its own facility, as of the May 15, 2024 page date.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a May 2024 plan. Whether the facility opened by Q1 2025 is not settled by this page.

assertions.value: The authors state that, as of March 2024, Quantum Computing Inc has secured its first offtake agreement with Comtech Telecommunications Corporation to produce wafers for its satellite communications.
quotes: As of March 2024, QCi has secured its first offtake agreement with Comtech Telecommunications Corporation to produce wafers for its satellite communications.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own commercial agreement. The page gives no terms.

assertions.value: The authors state that the Quantum Computing Inc U.S.-based foundry will enable components and integrated circuits for electro-optic modulators (printed as OEM in the text), frequency converters, periodically poled structures, and photonic integrated circuits (PIC).
quotes: QCi's U.S.-based foundry will enable components and integrated circuits for electro-optic modulators (OEM), frequency converters, periodically poled structures, and photonic integrated circuits (PIC).
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing the planned product scope of its own foundry.
assertions.reader_inference: The usual abbreviation for electro-optic modulator is EOM. The text prints OEM.

assertions.value: The authors state that TFLN is promising to become the silicon of the future, comparable to the silicon evolution that started in the 1940's, and that photonic integrated circuits on the TFLN platform are comparable to the 1970's developments that led to CMOS architectures.
quotes: Similar to the evolution of silicon technologies which started in the 1940's, TFLN is promising to become
is comparable to the developments and innovations in the 1970's that led to the advancement of Complementary Metal Oxide Semiconductor (CMOS) architectures
assertions.certainty_reason: A historical analogy offered as a forecast, with no evidence.

assertions.value: The authors state that the photonic-based computing machines being developed by Quantum Computing Inc leverage entropy and non-linear feedback instead of electrons, that QCi has recently begun deploying these machines, and that they use lithium niobate instead of silicon for computational tasks. No performance data is given.
quotes: photonic-based computing machines which are being developed by QCi are leveraging entropy, and non-linear feedback instead of electrons
These machines, which QCi has recently begun deploying, use lithium niobate instead of silicon for performing computational tasks.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor describing its own product with no benchmark or technical detail in the page.
assertions.reader_inference: The page does not say what problem class these machines solve or how they are measured.

assertions.value: The authors state that computing systems which use silicon chips seem like dinosaurs compared to TFLN nano photonics-based systems, and that using light instead of electricity is a key technological enabler likely to usher in a disruptive era of innovation.
quotes: Computing systems which use silicon chips seem like dinosaurs compared to TFLN nano photonics-based systems.
Using light instead of electricity is a key technological enabler likely to usher in a disruptive era of innovation.
assertions.certainty_reason: A rhetorical comparison with no data.
assertions.reader_inference: No metric, benchmark or workload is named for the comparison.

assertions.value: The authors state that scientists all over the world, including at Quantum Computing Inc, have demonstrated the ability to encode large amounts of information onto single photons, and that dense encoding and tight confinement make photons ideal for next generation optical computing engines. No citation is given.
quotes: scientists all over the world, including at QCi, have demonstrated the ability to encode large amounts of information onto single photons
The ability to densely encode information onto photons and confine them to very small spaces make them ideal for use in next generation optical computing engines.
assertions.certainty_reason: An unsourced statement about published demonstrations.

assertions.value: The authors state that nearly 43% of all energy used by large-scale computing facilities is spent on cooling, and that this is 110 Terawatts Hours of electricity used annually to cool data centers. No source is given.
quotes: nearly 43% of all energy used by large-scale computing facilities is spent on cooling.
Today, that is a staggering 110 Terawatts Hours of electricity which is used annually simply to cool data centers.
assertions.certainty_reason: Energy figures with no cited source, year or scope.
assertions.reader_inference: The figure is not tied to a year or a data source in the page, so it cannot be checked from the page alone.

assertions.value: The authors state that photons in action generate no heat, that photonic-based systems cannot overheat like electronic systems, and that such systems are therefore cheaper and easier to operate and generate less noise.
quotes: Photons in action generate no heat. As a result, photonic-based systems cannot overheat like electronic systems.
Not only does this make photonic-based systems cheaper and easier to operate, but also, they generate less
assertions.certainty_reason: An absolute claim with no measurement. The page does not address heat from lasers, drivers or control electronics.
assertions.reader_inference: The claim is stated without any qualification. The page does not discuss heat from the lasers, drive electronics and detectors that a photonic system also needs.

assertions.value: The authors state that Northrup Grumman, Raytheon, Samsung, IBM, Cisco, Dell and Qualcomm are all exploring TFLN, and that China Mobile, Tencent and Nippon Telegraph and Telephone compete for access and deployment of TFLN and photonic technology. No source is given.
quotes: Top innovators like Northrup Grumman, Raytheon, Samsung, IBM, Cisco, Dell, and Qualcomm are all exploring TFLN
their global competitors like China Mobile, Tencent, and Nippon Telegraph and Telephone compete for access and deployment of TFLN and photonic technology
assertions.certainty_reason: An unsourced list of third parties. The text spells Northrup, as printed.
